promptText: In the cache-aside pattern, why do most production systems evict the cache key on a write instead of updating it in place with the new value?
options: Updating in place opens a race where two interleaved writes, or a slow read that started before the write, can leave the cache permanently stranded on a stale value
Redis does not support updating an existing key's value, only deleting and re-creating it
Evicting is required because cache-aside cannot store values larger than a few kilobytes
Updating in place would bypass the TTL mechanism entirely, making entries never expire
explanation: If a slow read that began before a write finishes after the write has already updated the cache in place, it can overwrite the fresh value with a stale one; deleting the key and letting the next read repopulate it from the source of truth avoids that race, which is why delete-then-repopulate is the pattern almost every production system uses.

promptText: What is the core durability trade-off of the write-behind (write-back) caching pattern compared to write-through?
options: Writes are extremely fast because the caller never waits on the database, but a cache crash before the buffered writes flush means those writes are permanently lost
Write-behind guarantees stronger consistency than write-through because the cache and database are always updated together
Write-behind eliminates the need for any database at all once the cache is warmed
Write-behind is only usable for read-only data and cannot accept new writes
explanation: Write-behind returns success after writing only to the cache and flushes to the database asynchronously later, often batched; if the cache fails before that flush, the buffered writes are gone, which is why it needs a durable buffer and is reserved for workloads that can tolerate that risk in exchange for very low write latency.

promptText: What is the fundamental limitation of an in-process cache like Caffeine compared to a distributed cache like Redis, when running five application instances behind a load balancer?
options: Each instance has its own independent cache that can disagree with the others, and all of it is wiped whenever that instance restarts or redeploys
In-process caches cannot store more than a few dozen entries in total
In-process caches require a network round trip for every read, exactly like Redis
In-process caches cannot be used at all in a horizontally scaled system
explanation: An in-process cache lives inside one JVM's heap, so five instances effectively run five separate, independently-populated caches with no shared view, and each one loses all its entries on restart or redeploy, unlike a distributed cache that every instance shares and that survives individual instance restarts.

promptText: Why is Redis's maxmemory-policy noeviction considered a dangerous default for a service using Redis purely as a cache?
options: Once memory is full, Redis stops accepting new writes and returns an error to the client instead of quietly evicting an existing key to make room
noeviction causes Redis to silently corrupt existing keys once memory fills up
noeviction disables all read operations once the memory limit is reached, not just writes
noeviction is only a concern for Redis Cluster deployments, never for a single Redis node
explanation: noeviction means Redis rejects new writes outright once maxmemory is reached rather than evicting something, which is appropriate only when Redis is a primary datastore where silent data loss is worse than a rejected write; an actual cache almost always wants an eviction-based policy like allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu instead.

promptText: What problem does negative caching (caching a "not found" result) specifically solve?
options: It prevents repeated lookups for a key that genuinely does not exist from hitting the database on every single request, since a naive cache-aside implementation only populates the cache on a hit
It ensures that a deleted record is permanently and irreversibly removed from the database as well as the cache
It speeds up successful cache hits by pre-computing their values ahead of time
It prevents the cache from ever storing values larger than a configured size limit
explanation: Without negative caching, a nonexistent key (a typo'd ID, an enumeration attempt, a stale client reference) becomes a permanent, un-cacheable hole that always reaches the database on every request; caching the absence itself, typically with a shorter TTL than a real hit, closes that gap.

promptText: How does a CDN's caching role differ from an application-level cache like Redis or Caffeine in the same request path?
options: A CDN caches whole HTTP responses at edge locations for content that is the same for every user, potentially never reaching the origin at all, while Redis/Caffeine protect the database for content that is expensive to compute but varies by user
A CDN and Redis serve the exact same purpose and are interchangeable in any request path
A CDN can only cache database query results, not HTTP responses
Redis and Caffeine are only used for personalized content, while a CDN is only used for user sessions
explanation: A CDN sits in front of everything and caches the actual HTTP response for content identical across users (static assets, public pages), so a CDN hit never even reaches the application; Redis and Caffeine instead protect the database from load for content that is expensive to compute but often varies per user, which is a poor fit for CDN caching.

promptText: Why does Caffeine's default W-TinyLFU eviction policy outperform plain LRU when a one-off bulk scan (like a large batch job reading every record once) occurs?
options: W-TinyLFU uses a frequency sketch to decide whether a newly arriving key is popular enough to even be admitted, so cold one-time keys from a scan cannot flush out entries with a stronger frequency history the way plain LRU's pure recency ordering would
W-TinyLFU disables eviction entirely during a detected bulk scan
W-TinyLFU only evicts entries after they have been accessed at least once, unlike LRU
W-TinyLFU stores every entry that has ever been requested, so nothing is ever evicted
explanation: Plain LRU evicts based purely on recency, so a burst of one-time-use keys can flush out genuinely hot data simply because those cold keys were touched most recently; W-TinyLFU's frequency sketch decides admission based on historical popularity, with a small LRU-like window absorbing bursts, making it resistant to exactly this scan-poisoning failure mode.

promptText: In Redis Cluster, why does a Lua script or transaction that touches two different keys fail unless those keys are deliberately co-located with a hash tag like {user:123}?
options: Redis Cluster shards the keyspace into 16384 hash slots by CRC16(key) mod 16384, and a multi-key operation only works if every key involved hashes to the same slot, since the cluster does not coordinate a single command across multiple nodes
Lua scripts are disabled by default in Redis Cluster and must be explicitly re-enabled per key
Hash tags are required only when using AOF persistence, not RDB
Multi-key operations always work automatically in Redis Cluster regardless of which nodes own the keys
explanation: Each key maps to one of 16384 fixed hash slots owned by a specific node, and a command spanning multiple keys on different nodes cannot be executed atomically as one cluster-wide operation; wrapping the shared portion of the key in braces (a hash tag) ensures only that substring is hashed, forcing related keys onto the same slot and node.

promptText: A popular cache key expires and thousands of concurrent requests miss at the same instant. Which combination of techniques is the standard way to prevent this cache stampede from overwhelming the database?
options: A distributed lock so only one request recomputes the value while others wait or receive a stale value, combined with TTL jitter so keys populated together do not all expire at the same instant
Switching Redis's maxmemory-policy from allkeys-lru to noeviction
Increasing the number of Redis Cluster hash slots from 16384 to a higher number
Disabling the cache entirely so every request always queries the database directly
explanation: A lock (e.g. SET key value NX PX ttl) ensures only the first request recomputes the value while the rest wait briefly or get a stale value, and TTL jitter prevents synchronized expirations from causing coordinated misses in the first place; stale-while-revalidate and probabilistic early recomputation are the other standard complementary mitigations.

promptText: What is the precise distinction between read-through and cache-aside caching?
options: In read-through, the cache itself is configured with a loader and fetches from the source on a miss internally; in cache-aside, the application code explicitly checks the cache, calls the database on a miss, and writes the result back itself
Read-through is only usable with Redis, while cache-aside is only usable with an in-process cache like Caffeine
Cache-aside always uses a longer TTL than read-through by design
Read-through and cache-aside are two names for the exact same mechanism with no practical difference
explanation: The distinction is who owns miss-handling: read-through (Caffeine's get(key, loader), Spring's @Cacheable) delegates the fetch-on-miss logic to the cache abstraction itself via a configured loader, while hand-rolled cache-aside requires the application to spell out the if-null-then-fetch-then-put branch explicitly at every call site.

promptText: Redis Sentinel automates failover when a primary node dies. What guarantee does Sentinel explicitly NOT provide as part of that failover?
options: Zero data loss — because replication to replicas is asynchronous, any writes the primary had not yet replicated at the moment of failure are lost even after a replica is promoted
Automatic detection that the primary is unreachable
Promotion of a replica to become the new primary
Updating clients that discover the primary through Sentinel so they connect to the newly promoted node
explanation: Because Redis replication is asynchronous, the primary acknowledges writes without waiting for replica confirmation, so any writes not yet streamed to replicas when the primary dies are gone forever even though Sentinel successfully automates detecting the failure and promoting a replica; Sentinel provides automatic availability, not a zero-data-loss guarantee.

promptText: When designing a Redis-backed rate limiter for an API gateway, why do most production systems choose to fail open rather than fail closed if the backing Redis instance becomes unreachable?
options: The rate limiter's job is abuse prevention, not core functionality, so a brief window of unenforced limits during a Redis outage is a much smaller risk than turning a limiter outage into a full outage of the entire API
Failing open is required because Redis cannot be configured with a circuit breaker
Failing closed would cause the rate limiter to allow unlimited requests permanently, even after Redis recovers
Fail open and fail closed produce identical behavior for a rate limiter, so the choice does not matter
explanation: Failing closed (rejecting all requests when the limiter's store is unreachable) converts an outage of a protective, secondary system into an outage of the whole product, which is rarely the right trade for a component whose purpose is abuse prevention; failing open accepts a temporary lapse in enforcement instead, usually paired with a circuit breaker so requests fail fast rather than waiting out timeouts.

promptText: A team implements "write the database, then delete the cache key" for consistency. Why can a stale value still end up permanently stuck in the cache under this ordering, and what does the delayed double-delete pattern add to close most of that gap?
options: A reader that read a stale value from a lagging replica just before the write can repopulate the cache with that stale value after the post-write delete has already run; a second delete issued after a short delay clears out any such straggling repopulation
Write-then-delete has no race at all, so double-delete is purely a performance optimization unrelated to correctness
The race only occurs when using write-behind caching, never with write-database-then-delete-cache
Double-delete works by deleting the database record twice to guarantee it matches the cache
explanation: Even writing the database first narrows but does not eliminate the race: a read that started before the write and reads a stale value (especially from a lagging replica) can still repopulate the cache after the single post-write delete has already executed, stranding a stale value until TTL; the delayed second delete, timed to exceed typical replica lag and in-flight read duration, catches most of that straggling repopulation, though it remains a probabilistic mitigation rather than a guarantee.

promptText: A single product key is receiving disproportionate traffic on a Redis Cluster. The team adds more nodes to the cluster, but the overload on that one key persists. Why did scaling the cluster not help, and what is the correct fix?
options: Every request for that one key hashes to the same slot on the same single node regardless of cluster size, so adding nodes only spreads out other keys; the fix is local application-side caching of that key or splitting it into multiple key variants read round-robin across slots
Adding more nodes should have fixed it; the real problem must be an incorrectly configured maxmemory-policy
The problem is a cache stampede, so the fix is TTL jitter on that single key
Redis Cluster cannot handle more than 16384 total keys, which was exceeded
explanation: A hot key is a distribution problem, not a timing problem like a stampede: because every request for that key hashes to the same fixed slot owned by one node, that node's single CPU core bears the entire load no matter how many other nodes exist in the cluster; the standard fixes are local in-process caching of the hot key to absorb reads before they reach Redis, or key-splitting (storing several copies under different key variants) to spread the load across slots.

promptText: Kleppmann's critique of Redlock argues that acquiring a lock across a majority of independent Redis nodes still isn't safe as a hard correctness guarantee. What is the core of that critique, and what does it imply is the actual fix for correctness-critical locking?
options: Redlock's safety depends on real-time clock and process-pause assumptions (a GC pause or slow write can make a lock silently expire while the holder believes it still holds it), so the real fix is a fencing token that the protected resource itself validates, not simply adding more Redis nodes
Redlock is unsafe only because Redis itself has bugs in its SET NX PX implementation, which more nodes would eventually work around
The critique is that Redlock requires an even number of nodes, causing ties that more nodes alone would resolve
Kleppmann's critique has since been fully resolved by upgrading to Redis Cluster, making Redlock across multiple nodes provably safe
explanation: The critique is that a client can acquire a Redlock, then experience a long pause (GC, slow I/O) causing its lock to expire server-side while the client still believes it holds it and continues acting, and a majority-quorum lock across more Redis nodes does not address that clock/pause assumption; the actual mitigation for hard correctness is a monotonically increasing fencing token that the protected resource checks and rejects if an older token arrives after a newer one, closing the gap regardless of how many nodes back the lock.
